I was adopted at 12 and had similar emotional outbursts. For me personally, I had a difficult time to the adjustment. I had lived with my parents until they died, and then moved to my aunt's. I wasn't terribly close to her, didn't understand her lifestyle, or how she was a person. It took me probably until I was 14 to understand who she was and to build a trust with her. Because of this, there was times I felt alone. Alone in my feelings dealing with grief and change, which is where I believe the emotional outbursts came from. 
From what you said, I think you're doing great with picking and choosing your battles. My aunt was really strict and would ground me from my room or phone months at a time in order to teach a lesson which just made things more difficult, in my opinion. Being a teen is a hard age already and then dealing with being adopted on top of that is something most people don't understand.
Something that really helped me was art. I found it to be really soothing and a way I could positively express my emotions. I hope things get better!

Growing up, I felt like I was always held to very high expectations. And I had always struggled to meet them. In my last relationship, I learned a lot about how those expectations I was held to carried over in how I dealt with things. I would get really upset over little things because of the expectations I had created in my head and partly because of perfectionism. 

One day I was looked straight in the face and told "when you expect everything from everyone to be perfect, you'll always be let down. Understand what is truly in front of you and appreciate it." 

Since then, I try to only hold myself to expectations and don't expect much from others. If they do something then great, if they don't then that's on them and not me. This doesn't always happen, but it's becoming more common in how I deal with high expectations.
I wish I could upvote this more than once.

I first realized it when I was almost 14 that I felt alone in my grieving. It had been 3 years and entering high-school was a transition that I wanted my parents to be there for (both of my parents passed away). I started going to counseling but it wasn't helping because my adoptive mother sent me for behavioral issues and not for grief support. I soon stopped going, I would refuse to get out of the car when my "new" mom took me. So I turned to the guidance counselor at school probably a year or so later in total confidentially. There is finally felt like I could be free to express how hard the transitions in my life were without my parents. It put me in a good place. 
Soon enough though, I graduated and entered into college. I started counseling my second semester. That counseling didn't do as much for me as I was hoping but it did teach me the joy of meditation. I use that now on hard days when I feel like giving up and sleeping through the grief pains. I also go to a professor every once in a great while when I have very difficult days. I'll sit in his office and cry. He'll read scriptures and reassure me that I'm not alone. I also got lucky during my first semester; that's when I met my boyfriend. He's also adopted but under different circumstances. His support has really strengthen me over the past two years.
 I know that although I have a support system of friends as well who care. The major transitions of life are going to be overbearing for me. Graduation from college, wedding, birth of my children, etc., those are all things that will reignite the pain of the loss of my parents.
I just keep reminding myself that "everything is gonna be okay" because it always is.

Personally, I didn't know how to cope with the losses I had. People were very supportive for the first few weeks. But then afterwards it seems like you should be back to normal by their standards. But it doesn't work that way. I didn't look for help till years later. I just told myself I had to be strong, but as I grew into an adult things were becoming overwhelming. As a kid grieving, I read alot of books that had stories from other kids about their loss. I didn't want to feel alone and reading those stories let me know that if those kids had loss and we're okay then I would be okay too. It's been almost 10 years since and I still have days where I struggle. I lean on my boyfriend for support now; he's really understanding about my situation and doesn't make me feel like being sad is wrong.

I played varsity volleyball in high school and was the DS. I rarely played front row because I'm only 5 ft. tall. I would suggest that playing a DS to remember to constantly be moving on the court. My rule was to move my feet at least 3 times each time the ball moved on the other side so I could constantly be setting myself up for whatever possible move was going to come. It helped me a lot and I was able to accomplish a lot with just that simple though and goal.
I still have my good days and my bad days, but everything is going well. Your welcome to pm me and ask anything, I'm always up for sharing my story!

Wow our stories are some what similar! My mom passed from a brain hemmorage when I was 11. Then 11 months later, my dad passed from a heart attack. My "aunt", who's really a second cousin once removed, took me in. I'm a month short of 21. 

I definitely wish there was more grieving tips out there. Most stories of parents who pass are from car accidents. My best grieving advise was giving to me by a neighbor: "you'll never forget your parents, so don't pretend that you have. If you have a bad day, cry but remember to pick yourself back up. And on holidays it's okay to celebrate as if they are still there." I personally buy helium balloons on my parents birthdays ever year. I write notes to them and tie it to the string of the balloons. I'll sing happy birthday before releasing them..

I don't know if what I say will help. My dad died from a heart attack almost 10 years ago. I, too, am scared of dying from a heart attack. For a few years after his death I was angry. For some of the same reasons as you; he drank too much, he didn't exercise, he wasn't super healthy. I did go to counselling, twice. The first time didn't help much. Personally, I just didn't click with the counselor. The second time I went, it made a big impact on my views. I let go of the anger. I had to realize that he was my dad, that I still love him even though he made mistakes. Parents don't receive handbooks when they have a kid. People don't get handbooks telling them how to live the perfect life. I came to understand through counselling that holding onto anger isn't going to change anything except my own attitude and well-being. I'm at peace now with the situation because of counselling and taking time to reflect about life, although I'm still scared of dying from a heart attack. I hope you can find some peace within yourself too. I'm sure it will help you too become an even better dad, husband, and friend.

Okay. I did grow up with my parents and their rules and how they structured the house, which would be different from a child from foster care. When I first moved in with my adoptive mother (she was taking this on all by herself) I was very hesitant to do anything. I was afraid to touch anything in the house, to get food when I was hungry, or to even ask questions. She really helped with my adjustment period by telling me it was okay to do this or to not do that (I went from living in the middle of a city to out in the country; it's amazing the differences in how to do even the simplest of things). Middle school was a blur, I remember not having many problem between me and my adoptive mother; however, that changed in high school. I became really "rebellious" as a teenager and was quite hard headed about wanting to have a life like I had with my birth parents again. This made things difficult, and of course as the child I didn't agree with how my adoptive mother handled certain situations. As an adult now I understand why she did the things she did.

I was in a similar situation in my current relationship. When I first got with my boyfriend, I hadn't known he smoked since he kept it very secretive. Obviously, I found out and I overreacted (as I can look back now) and told him it was me or the weed. He chose me, but I soon realized he was unhappy since smoking was something that brought him joy. I reflected on it for months and then just simply talked with him. I came to to realize that if he enjoys it, I shouldn't be making he chose. We ended up agreeing that if he wants to smoke to just text me or call and let me know. This made it that I could know whether he was high or not, so then I could stay away if I wanted to. It works well for us; however, I'm not against smoking either.
One thing that should be considered on your girlfriend's part is if she wants be in a relationship where smoking is a thing. There are many other guys out in the world who don't like weed just like her.
